item.title: Calculate checksum in Ruby
item.description:
Every developer has faced computing SHA256 checksums for files in their project at some point. For instance, you might need to search for exact file matches or, conversely, prevent duplicate uploads of an existing file. In Ruby, you can use the Digest::SHA256 class for this. But there’s a catch: the built-in method only works for files that already exist on the file system:

require 'digest'
require 'stringio'
require 'tempfile'

src = StringIO.new('Hello, Ruby!')
f = Tempfile.new
f.sync = true
IO.copy_stream(src, f)
Digest::SHA256.file(f.path).hexdigest

However, since a file uploaded by a user is typically represented as a stream (IO) in your web application, Ruby surprisingly doesn’t have a built-in way to calculate a hash directly from a stream. item.title: Temporary files and folders in Ruby
item.description: If you’ve been using Ruby for a while, you’ve likely come across Tempfile in your projects. In short, it creates a temporary file in the system’s /tmp directory. From there, you can pass it as an argument to other methods just like a regular file (I mostly see this used in image manipulation gems like mini_magick). If you pass a block, the file is automatically deleted after execution. If not, you’ll need to close and unlink it manually. Keep in mind that Tempfile.create returns an instance of File, not Tempfile. What you might have missed is that Ruby also provides Dir.mktmpdir, which creates a temporary directory (also in /tmp). This is especially useful when writing integration tests where you need to generate multiple temporary files for downstream steps. Dir.mktmpdir returns the path to the temporary folder, allowing you to create files inside it using standard methods like File.write.

item.title: Text data section in Ruby
item.description: If you code in Ruby, you can discover new features practically every day. For instance, one of the coolest features I stumbled upon in the documentation just a few days ago (despite writing Ruby for over 10 years!) is that you can embed text data directly inside your source file. All you need to do is place an __END__ marker at the bottom of the file. Anything you write after that line can be read right out of the DATA object inside the same source file. Under the hood, the DATA constant is simply an open file stream of your current (entrypoint) file in read-only mode, with its pointer positioned immediately after the __END__ line.
